content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission. In this unit, you will read short passages about classroom discussions and learn how people share their thoughts. You will discover practical ways to agree with positive or negative statements, and how to express different opinions politely and constructively.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Short agreement responses (So do I, Neither do I) and polite transition phrases for different opinions.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words related to opinions, perspectives, and respectful communication.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming for general themes in dialogue and scanning for specific agreement or disagreement expressions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 reading texts about group discussions.
Locate specific details such as agreement and disagreement expressions in conversations.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with short responses and polite phrasing.

contextWarmup.prompt: When your friend has a different opinion than you during a conversation, what is the best way to respond?
options: Listen to their view, acknowledge it politely, and explain your perspective calmly.
Shout loudly so everyone knows your idea is better.
Walk away immediately without saying anything.
contextWarmup.explanation: Listening and responding politely keeps the discussion constructive and friendly.

rules: To agree with a positive statement, use 'So do I' or 'Me too'. Example: A: 'I like pizza.' B: 'So do I!'
To agree with a negative statement, use 'Neither do I' or 'Me neither'. Example: A: 'I don't like cold weather.' B: 'Neither do I!'
To show full agreement, use phrases like 'I totally agree', 'I agree with you', 'Absolutely', 'That's true', or 'You're right'.
To disagree politely, start with acknowledgment phrases such as 'I see what you mean, but...', 'That's a valid point, however...', or 'I understand, but...'.
Use a friendly tone and open body language when you disagree to keep the discussion positive and constructive.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Using 'So am I' for Regular Verbs
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up auxiliary verbs when agreeing with simple present statements. If the sentence uses 'like' or 'play', you must use 'So do I', not 'So am I'.
commonTrap.wrong: A: I play tennis. B: So am I.
commonTrap.correct: A: I play tennis. B: So do I.

content.passageTitle: The Class Discussion on School Clubs
paragraphs: Yesterday afternoon, the students in class A2 had an interesting discussion about after-school clubs. Anna stood up and shared her opinion. She said that the school photography club was the most exciting activity because students could learn new creative skills. Mark listened carefully to her presentation. He raised his hand and replied, 'I see what you mean about photography, but I think the coding club is more useful for our future careers.'

Sarah smiled and joined the conversation. She said, 'That is a valid point, Mark. However, I believe we should also consider sports clubs because physical health is very important.' Anna nodded and said, 'So do I! I enjoy playing basketball too.' The teacher was very happy to see everyone communicating with respect, sharing different perspectives, and having a constructive conversation without any arguments.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Polite Agreement & Constructive Disagreement

content.summary: Learn how to write polite agreement and constructive disagreement responses in discussions, emails, and comments using clear phrases and proper punctuation.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Short Agreement Phrases
blueprintItems.formula: So + auxiliary verb + pronoun (for positive) / Neither + auxiliary verb + pronoun (for negative)
blueprintItems.example: A: 'I love reading books.' B: 'So do I!'

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Full Agreement Sentences
blueprintItems.formula: I totally agree / I agree with you + that + clause
blueprintItems.example: I totally agree that learning English is useful.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Polite Disagreement Openings
blueprintItems.formula: Polite phrase + comma + but / however + contrasting idea
blueprintItems.example: I see what you mean, but team sports are more fun.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the pronoun 'I' and the first word of every sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: so do i, because science is interesting.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: So do I, because science is interesting.
mechanicsRules.why: The pronoun 'I' and sentence beginnings must always be capitalized in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after introductory agreement or disagreement phrases.
mechanicsRules.badExample: That is true I think online classes are helpful.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: That is true, I think online classes are helpful.
mechanicsRules.why: Introductory phrases and independent clauses require proper punctuation like commas.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use exclamation marks or periods correctly at the end of short agreement replies.
mechanicsRules.why: Exclamation marks show enthusiasm in short agreements.
